nameStory: The 'sundial' in sundial lupine comes from how the plant's distinctive palm-shaped leaves track the sun throughout the day, rotating like the hand of a sundial. This sun-following behavior, called heliotropism, helps the plant maximize photosynthesis as shadows shift across the forest floor.
description: Sundial lupine is a striking wildflower that grows 1-2 feet tall with distinctive hand-shaped leaves that look like green fans. In late spring and early summer, it sends up tall spikes of blue-purple pea-like flowers that bloom from bottom to top. This native perennial belongs to the legume family, the same group as beans and peas, and you can see the family resemblance in both the flowers and the fuzzy seed pods that follow.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Distinctive palm-shaped leaves with 7-11 narrow leaflets radiating from a central point like fingers on a hand. The leaflets feel smooth and have a slightly waxy texture, and they noticeably track the sun's movement throughout the day.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tall spikes of blue to purple pea-like flowers that bloom from the bottom up over several weeks. Each flower has the classic legume shape with an upright 'banner' petal and lower 'keel' petals, and they have a light, sweet fragrance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms colonies from underground rhizomes, often appearing in patches. Plants typically reach 1-2 feet tall with multiple flower spikes rising above the foliage on sturdy, slightly hairy stems.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Fuzzy, flattened seed pods about 1-2 inches long that turn brown and twist open with an audible 'pop' when ripe, scattering hard black seeds. The pods feel velvety to the touch when young.

habitat: Found in dry, sandy or rocky soils in open woodlands, clearings, and along woodland edges throughout New England. Prefers acidic soils and partial shade to full sun, often growing with oak trees, blueberries, and other plants that thrive in nutrient-poor conditions. Commonly seen in pine barrens and areas with well-drained, sandy soils.

seasonality.spring: New palm-shaped leaves emerge bright green in early spring, and flower buds begin forming on tall spikes by late spring. The distinctive leaf shape makes identification easy even before blooming begins.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from late May through July, with blue-purple flower spikes at their showiest. Seeds develop in fuzzy pods that ripen and pop open by late summer, scattering seeds with audible snaps.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow and begin to die back, while empty seed pods remain on stems. The plant goes dormant but may leave dried stalks visible through early fall.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with no above-ground growth visible. Look for dried seed pods and stems from the previous year, but the plant overwinters entirely underground via rhizomes.

funFact: Sundial lupine is the only host plant for the endangered Karner blue butterfly caterpillars, which means this single wildflower species determines whether these beautiful butterflies can survive in an area - making every lupine patch a potential butterfly nursery!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with large-leaved lupine, an escaped garden plant that's much taller (3-5 feet) with broader leaflets and denser flower spikes. Memory trick: sundial lupine is the 'petite native' while large-leaved lupine is the 'big garden escape' - if it's taller than your waist, it's probably the non-native one.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'Indian beet,' this plant is not related to actual beets and the roots should not be eaten. Like many legumes, sundial lupine contains alkaloids that can be toxic to livestock and humans, so it's best appreciated with your eyes rather than your taste buds.
compareHints: Sundial lupine is much smaller and more delicate than its cousin large-leaved lupine, which commonly escapes from gardens. Sundial lupine rarely exceeds 2 feet tall with narrower leaflets and sparser flower spikes, while large-leaved lupine towers at 3-5 feet with broader leaflets and dense, showy flower clusters. If you see lupines in a wild setting that look like they belong in a formal garden, they're probably the non-native large-leaved species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its native New England cousin, the sundial lupine, large-leaved lupine is much more robust in every way - taller stems, bigger leaves, and showier flower spikes.
